title: Finally, the Fun Part Begins
dateline: The Storm Citadel, behind the gateway.
mood: Behind the torn sky something vast wakes, and on the bell tower a girl with a lollipop starts to smile.

hero.alt: Selena in her school uniform holds a lollipop under a storm sky and lifts one hand lazily, her dragon-shaped machine Silverbolt rising beside her; then she sits on the edge of a high roof with her legs over the drop, Silverbolt crouched at her side.

segs.t: Obsidia stood at the top of the steps in her throne hall, deep among the hanging blocks. Behind her the throne climbed out of sight, bone over bone. The body had grown it for her when she woke.
One hand rested on it. Under her palm it was warm, and it hummed.
Through the eyes of the gray Enders on her outer blocks, she watched the Mother Matrix withdraw.

It came through the star of human sky slowly, its wings half folded. Magenta still glowed along the seam where its chest plates had shut over the wound. It passed below her keel without turning its head, and went on into the dark, back to where it healed.
All morning the Enders on the city’s platforms had shown her everything, and understood none of it.

A machine of her kind’s plates had stood up in front of the body’s beam. In the hollow it had stayed dead under her own hand. A human’s belief had lit it. Then every Ender on those platforms had turned on Vexana.
After that, two lights had gone into the open chest together. The black point at the center of the mouth had taken them.
Nothing made of matter ever comes back out,
she had told the girl on her prow.
Two lights had come back out. The body had given way before them.
She did not know how.
On every world she had helped to end, nothing had ever wounded the Will’s body. Today two human girls had.
She had known Vexana would turn since the day she looked at that sleeve. The body giving ground was another thing.
The violet in her eyes brightened.
“Merely a prelude to the end,” she said to the empty hall.
Her weapon came gliding out of the dark and settled under her free hand. She drew her claws down it, and it went still.

media.alt: In a dark hall a tall jointed column climbs out of sight above a figure on a dais while a long, bladed weapon crawls across the floor to her; then, close, she reaches back and runs her claws along the creature of a weapon at her side.

segs.t: The pulse told her where her pawn was: on a tower over the humans’ Academy. It lived. It had obeyed no call of hers, and for days it had sent her no word.
“Destruction is mine to command, yet my finest creation... has gone off-script,” she told the weapon.

blocks.caption: Destruction is mine to command, yet my finest creation... has gone off-script.

segs.t: The day before, she had planned for both outcomes. If the body finished them, she would watch. If not, she would go in once the mouth was clear.
The mouth was clear. The field slept in the bone under her hand.
The last call could wait. First the pawn must show its own shape.
Her fingers closed on the bone.
Through the whole ship, block by block, something woke. The storm wound in close around the hull. Far along the spine the red heart burned brighter. The prow tipped toward the star of sky.
“Let us begin the final purge,” said Obsidia.
The Storm Citadel began to move.
The bell tower.
Rain came across the tiles in gusts. Selena sat at the very edge in her school uniform, both legs hanging over the air. The lollipop in her cheek had worn down by half. She was making it last.
Silverbolt crouched against her hip. Water ran off its plates in strings.
Out over the bay, the mouth had hung empty since the Matrix went back. Its cloud kept coming, black, and spread low across the water.
The hum reached her first.
It came up through the tiles into her bones before she saw a thing. Deep and huge, from over the water.
She knew it. Every Ender she had ever passed had carried a small piece of it. This was the whole of it.

It was the hum of the night of the mud, when she stood barefoot in a dark street. That night it had come down from a black cloud over the bay. Violet light had moved in its belly, and something vast had waited inside.
Home,
said her bones, the way they had in the mud.
You and everybody else,
thought Selena.
The mouth’s rim had been magenta all morning. Now it burned red, and its four points dragged wider. The sky along its edges tore, and kept tearing.
The pull in her cells had moved. It came from just behind that red, closer than it had ever been. The huntress had come.
“Finally... the fun part begins,” said Selena.
She was smiling. It was none of the ones she kept.
Something came through, wrapped in its own storm. Coming all the way through took a long time.
It was a ship, and a whole city hung from it upside down. Its black towers pointed down at the bay, their edges cut to blades. Deep in the middle of it, a red-orange heart burned.
So that’s what was inside.
No purple portals this time. Smaller ships poured out of the mouth around the big one, dark and quick, dozens of them. Each one hummed too, a small sharp note under the deep one.
Over the bay their bellies opened, and Enders dropped out of them by the hundred. More leapt from the lowest towers of the great ship.

blocks.caption: No portals this time. A ship, and smaller ships around it.

media.alt: Over a city of towers a red four-pointed tear burns open in the sky while Selena and Silverbolt watch from a rooftop; then a huge dark ship of blade-edged towers hangs inside the red tear among smaller ships, and Enders leap from its lower edges and drop past its burning underside.

segs.t: From up here she could see where every one came down. On the waterfront roofs, still smoking from the first wave. Along the bay road. In the wards past the old market, on streets she had raced through on storm nights. On towers far inland, almost at the dome’s landward edge.
On the platforms the frontline turned to meet them. A gold light, a violet one. Cyan along a pair of blades and a cannon.
“It’s the ship from the oldest record,” said Chang’e in her ear, fast and thin. “The Storm Citadel.”
“Mobile support,” said Lesley. “Report.”
Selena let the commander’s voice go by. The pull she let burn.
Beside her, Silverbolt’s head came up. It turned toward the ship and stayed there.
It only ever moved when some part of her meant it to.
She laid her palm flat on its brow and pressed, until its head came down against her knee.

Then she looked the Storm Citadel over for a way in, a seam or a door. The pull ran straight into the ship. Among the blocks it spread out, and she lost it. Block after block, the ship gave her nothing.
Fine,
she thought.
Never move first. Let the huntress show her hand.
The Storm Citadel cleared the mouth. Slowly it turned inland, toward the Academy. Its black cloud rolled out across the bay ahead of it. The rain on the tiles came harder.
Selena took the lollipop out of her mouth and looked at it. Then she put it back.
“Not yet,” she told it.
